# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>

# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and the Halden Subset

This is the most informative document so far. It answers several of the open questions directly:

- **Durability:** the gain was still present at 24 months, measured against a control group.
- **Mechanism:** a registered mediation test, specified before outcomes were known, was run on the meetings hypothesis.
- **Unrecorded work:** a second hours measure from system logs was added.
- **Cost of coverage-bound work:** the county estimated the cost of restoring service.

It also settles a factual question I raised about the meta-analysis. The four long-run studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" was weaker than it looked.

The arithmetic checks out:

| Item | Calculation | Reported | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% | ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% | ✓ |
| CIs on the log scale | e.g. 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) is symmetric | | ✓ |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% | ✓ |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 | +11.8% | ✓ |
| Control-adjusted meeting cut | (7.4 − 3.9) − (7.2 − 7.0) | 3.3 hours | ✓ |

There is one significant inconsistency between the hours accounting and the mediation results, discussed in point 1. Several framing points also need correcting.

## 1. The meetings cut appears to account for almost all of the per-hour gain, not 47%

The paper's own figures allow a rough accounting check.

| Step | Figure |
|---|---|
| Treated baseline hours (from the 9-month report) | about 37.9 per week |
| Of which recurring meetings | 7.4 hours |
| Non-meeting time at baseline | about 30.5 hours |
| Hours at 24 months (−12%, timesheets) | about 33.4 |
| Of which meetings | 3.9 hours |
| **Non-meeting time at 24 months** | **about 29.5 hours (−3%)** |
| Output per FTE | −3.4% |
| **Output per non-meeting hour** | **roughly unchanged (about 0%)** |

Using the −11% log figure gives about −1% instead. Either way, about 80% of the cut in hours came out of meeting time. Staff produced about the same output per hour of non-meeting work as before. On this accounting, the per-hour gain comes almost entirely from removing meeting hours from the denominator, which leaves little room for fatigue (18%) or the "unexplained" 35%.

This doesn't invalidate the registered mediation analysis. It estimates something different: how variation in the mediators across offices relates to variation in the outcome, under strong assumptions. But the two approaches point to quite different conclusions, and the paper should reconcile them. This is an approximation on my part, because it uses the 9-month baseline and treats difference-in-differences changes as simple changes.

**What the log measure includes matters here.** The log measure is described as recording time "working on cases." If that were literally true, it would exclude meetings. Cutting meetings would then barely reduce log hours, and log hours should have fallen by about 3%, not 11%. The 11% fall suggests logs capture total logged-in time, meetings included. The paper should define the measure precisely, because the meaning of "output per log-measured hour" depends on it.

## 2. The mediation result is stronger evidence than before, but "confirms" overstates it

The registration is genuine: it was filed at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available, with the mediators and outcome specified in advance. That answers Varga and Holm's "post hoc" objection. However:

- **Mediation needs an assumption that cannot be checked.** It requires no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. Meeting cuts were not randomised, and offices whose managers cut more meetings may simply be better run. The limitations section notes this. The summary's "confirms" does not.
- **"A larger sample of office-months" is pseudo-replication.** Repeated months from the same office are correlated. The effective sample is still 14 offices, and the intervals of 28–66% and 2–34% may be too narrow unless they were clustered appropriately. The paper doesn't say.
- **The shares assume the pathways are independent.** Fewer meetings could themselves reduce fatigue, so splitting the gain into 47%, 18% and 35% may not be meaningful.

**It also partly vindicates Varga and Holm.** If the gain comes mainly from removing low-value meeting time, it is a real efficiency gain for the employer, and quality held steady (3.2% vs 3.0%). But it is not "staff work faster when rested." Varga and Holm were wrong that nothing remains. They were closer to right that people don't become more productive *per hour of actual work*.

## 3. The summary overstates the decline by mixing measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% is from logs. The like-for-like comparison, which the body text correctly gives, is 12.5% → 9.8%.

Further points on decay:

- **The decline is not statistically established.** The intervals (+6.9% to +18.4% and +4.6% to +15.2%) overlap almost entirely.
- **Only two time points are reported.** Without the 12- and 18-month values, it's impossible to tell whether the gain has levelled off or is still falling. "Declined but not disappeared" is accurate *at 24 months*. It says nothing about later.
- **Some of the "decline" may be the control group improving.** Two of the seven control offices ran a meeting audit at month 15 and gained 4.1% in output per hour. That would lift the control average by roughly 1 point (2/7 × 4.1%) from month 15 onwards and shrink the measured treatment effect by a similar amount. Part of the move from 12.5% to 9.8% could therefore be contamination of the control group rather than fading. The paper treats the audit as a side observation, but it bears directly on the decay estimate.

## 4. The unplanned observation deserves more weight than the paper gives it

Two control offices cut meetings by 2.1 hours *without reducing hours* and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. Treated offices cut about 3.3 hours of meetings (control-adjusted), and roughly 4.0 points of their gain (47% of 8.5%) is attributed to the meetings pathway. On this tiny sample, the meeting audit produced as much per hour of meetings cut as the hours reduction did.

The authors rightly hedge: two offices, no control, and the hours cut may be what *prompts* reorganisation and makes it stick. But for an employer, this is the most decision-relevant finding in the series. It suggests that much of the gain might be available without the costs of reduced hours. The obvious next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, a meeting audit at standard hours, and control.

## 5. The cost analysis is done for counters but not case-processing

The counter estimate is useful. The county estimated +12% staff and +9% cost per contact, which is consistent if wages are about three-quarters of total cost (12% × 0.75 ≈ 9%). It was also a real decision that confirms the meta-analysis's finding for coverage-bound work.

Case-processing gets no equivalent:

- Output per FTE fell 3.4% at full pay, so unit labour cost rose by at least 3.5%.
- Paid overtime would add more. Timesheet hours imply roughly 3 overtime hours per person per week, so at 24 months the cost implications I estimated for the 9-month report (roughly 15–18% under assumed overtime terms) probably still apply.

This is the remaining question that matters most for employers, and the paper leaves it unanswered.

## 6. The Halden subset: selection, framing and authorship

- **Selection at several stages.** Of the 70 organisations enrolled, 9 withdrew. Of the 61 who completed the pilot, 23 had records and 14 of those agreed to follow-up. Three of the 14 reverted and 11 continued. Refusers may differ from the organisations that took part. The authors call the 11 "survivors twice over," which understates the selection.
- **"Upper bound" is not technically correct.** Selection probably biases the figure upwards. But with no control group, two to three years of background productivity growth or demand changes could push the output index either way. "Probably optimistic" is more accurate than "upper bound."
- **The baseline hours figure is suspicious.** The continuers' baseline of 40.3 hours matches exactly the figure Varga and Holm reported for the 27 organisations with time tracking. That may be coincidence, or a pooled baseline applied to a subgroup. If the 11's own baseline differs, the hours reduction and per-hour gain change.
- **The reversion category has been widened.** The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is a discretionary-sector organisation under the meta-analysis's coding. Extending "coverage" to include client responsiveness is reasonable, but it blurs the clean distinction between discretionary and coverage-bound work.
- **Halden's own claims are not addressed.** R. Okafor, the Halden lead author, is a co-author here. Section 5 addresses the claims of the re-analysis and the meta-analysis. It does not address Halden's: the misreported attrition, the "sector-general" conclusion, the 23.4% headline, or the fatigue explanation, which the mediation analysis now ranks second. A brief acknowledgement would be appropriate.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%).** The form of the schedule is still not stated. If it is a four-day week, much of this fall is mechanical, as I noted for the 9-month report.
- **Varga and Holm's month-ten extrapolation.** The rebuttal is fair, but it rests on a different population (Varden staff, not Halden staff). Varga and Holm's argument was general, so the rebuttal holds against it. The energy measure was never shown to track output in any case.
- **The meta-analysis critique is correct and important.** The meta-analysis's own moderators implied that four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies would show inflated, non-decaying estimates.

## How the five documents fit together

| Question | Best current answer | Main source | Remaining uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | about +8–10% at 24 months | Varden follow-up (logs, RCT) | One employer, 7 v 7 offices |
| Durability | Some decline (12.5 → 9.8), not to zero | Varden follow-up | Two time points; control contamination |
| Coverage-bound work | Output −9 to −11%; restoring service costs about +9% | Varden, meta-analysis | Alternative implementations untested |
| Mechanism | Mainly removing meeting time; fatigue secondary | Registered mediation, plus accounting | Mediation assumptions; possibly nearly all meetings |
| Necessity of the hours cut | Unknown; meeting audit alone gave +4% | Two control offices | No reorganise-only arm |
| Cost per unit, discretionary work | Not reported; likely higher | (inferred) | Overtime terms |

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- A real, durable-to-24-months gain in output per actual hour of about 8–10% in case-processing. The comparison was randomised and the output data record-based, with system-log hours.
- The gain declined somewhat from 9 months, but did not vanish by month ten as Varga and Holm's extrapolation implied.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" rested entirely on studies with inflated designs.
- Coverage-bound work with unchanged staffing patterns degrades service, and restoring it costs money.

**Needs correction or qualification:**
- The summary's 12.5% → 8.5% comparison mixes measures. The like-for-like figure is 12.5% → 9.8%.
- "Confirms" overstates a mediation result that relies on assumptions which cannot be checked, and on pseudo-replicated office-months.
- Simple accounting suggests meetings explain most or all of the gain, not 47%. The definition of log hours needs clarifying.
- The control-office meeting audit contaminates the decay estimate and deserves more prominence.
- There is no cost analysis for case-processing.
- The Halden subset is "probably optimistic" rather than an "upper bound," and Halden's own errors go unacknowledged.

**The key open question has changed.** It is no longer whether reduced hours raise productivity. It is whether the gain comes from the reduced hours, or from reorganisation that the reduced hours trigger. Only a trial with a reorganisation-only arm can answer that, and the answer determines whether employers need to cut hours at all.
